chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a sacrificial animal for his 'Umrat al-Tamattu'. He brought it to his family, tied it, then released it, and it perished. Would it suffice him, or should he repeat (offer another)? He (peace be upon him) said: 'It would not suffice him unless he has no financial strength to offer another.'

key_terms.لَا قُوَّةَ بِهِ عَلَيْهِ: He has no financial strength/capacity for it
key_terms.لِمُتْعَتِهِ: For his 'Umrat al-Tamattu' (a specific type of pilgrimage)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if the sacrificial animal for Umrah dies before slaughter?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that if a pilgrim’s sacrificial animal dies after being tied and released but before reaching the slaughtering place, the sacrifice is invalid unless the owner is financially incapacitated. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the animal's presence and readiness for slaughter as a condition for validity, distinguishing it from cases where the animal perishes during the journey. The exception for financial inability highlights the principle of ease (taysir) in Islamic law, ensuring that those who cannot afford a replacement are not burdened with double sacrifice.
